hints: Notice the shape of the vertical velocity against time graph in each labelled region, especially whether velocity is increasing, constant or decreasing.
Recall that the gradient of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and link acceleration direction to net force using $F_{net} = W - D$ with $W$ downwards and drag $D$ upwards.
Look for the region with a steep negative gradient where rapid deceleration requires a large upward net force, meaning $D$ must be much larger than $W$.
walkthrough: Identify the motion from the graph: region A shows velocity increasing with decreasing gradient, region B shows constant high velocity, region C shows velocity falling steeply, region D shows constant low velocity.
State the forces: weight $W$ acts downwards and is almost constant, drag due to air resistance $D$ acts upwards and increases when speed or parachute area increases.
Use Newton's second law for downward positive: $W - D = ma$. The sign of $a$ is the sign of the gradient of the velocity-time graph.
In region C the gradient is large and negative, so $a$ is large and upwards. Then $W - D$ must be large and negative.
That requires $D - W$ to be large and positive, so $D$ is much greater than $W$ during the rapid deceleration just after the parachute opens. This is option C.

options.A: In region A velocity is increasing, so net force is downwards and weight must be greater than air resistance.
options.B: In region B velocity is constant at first terminal velocity, so net force is zero and air resistance equals weight.
options.C: In region C velocity decreases rapidly, so there is a large upward net force and air resistance must be much larger than weight.
options.D: In region D velocity is again almost constant at a lower terminal velocity, so air resistance is again approximately equal to weight.
